summary:
New Mexico stands under the national framework of the United States, and that framework is the first exposure a trans visitor faces. Since January 2025, Executive Order 14168 has required federal identity documents to reflect sex assigned at birth. The State Department stopped processing the X marker and any marker not matching sex assigned at birth; new passport applications are processed only as M or F according to the supporting documents submitted, while passports already issued with an X remain valid until they expire. Trans and nonbinary travellers report passports confiscated or blocked at application, with some left stranded abroad. The ACLU has sued the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs, Lambda Legal maintains guidance on how name and gender changes interact with federal records, and the Supreme Court recently allowed the State Department to proceed with its changed treatment of trans passports.

Entry and screening follow national rules regardless of which state the visitor lands in. Executive Order 14201 of 5 February 2025 was followed on 25 February 2025 by a State Department announcement that trans athletes seeking to enter the country to compete in women's sporting events will be refused visas and flagged internally under the code 'SWS25'; the same announcement states that an applicant who declares a gender other than sex assigned at birth may be treated as fraud and barred permanently. At checkpoints, secondary screening, body scanners and pat-downs can expose a traveller's trans status to officers and other passengers, according to the National Center for Transgender Equality's know-your-rights guide, which sets out how to request screening matching one's presentation.

Facility use and identity documents are regulated state by state, so the rules encountered inside New Mexico differ from those in states that restrict them. State bathroom bans applying to trans people in K-12 schools and some government buildings are in force in nine states and one territory, with trans bathroom use a criminal offence in certain circumstances in some jurisdictions, while twenty-nine states, four territories and the District of Columbia have no such ban. Enforcement has occurred: in April 2025 a trans student was arrested and handcuffed after using a women's restroom at a state capitol, identified by civil-rights attorneys as the first known arrest under a state bathroom-restriction law. Kansas has enacted a law invalidating birth certificates and driver's licences that do not bear sex assigned at birth and barring trans residents from changing those markers, described by rights groups as a template other legislatures are following. Multiple foreign governments, at least eight European countries including Finland and Denmark, adjusted travel guidelines for their trans and nonbinary citizens after the federal document and data rules, and a national legal risk assessment dated 13 July 2026 identifies four states now designated do-not-travel for trans people.

Within that national picture, New Mexico sits in the fifteen-state 'Most Protective' tier of the July 2026 national legal-risk ranking, alongside California, Colorado, Connecticut, Hawaii, Illinois, Massachusetts, Maryland, Minnesota, New Jersey, New York, Oregon, Rhode Island, Vermont and Washington. The ranking is built from a rubric applied over thousands of tracked anti-trans bills covering youth-care bans, bathroom bans, birth-certificate and driver-licence restrictions and the end of legal recognition, and it records that the laws of the protective-tier states have gone above and beyond in safeguarding trans rights.

New Mexico also operates a shield or refuge law, listed by the Movement Advancement Project's Transgender Healthcare Equality Map as 'State has shield law or executive order 2023'. The law protects patients and providers from civil or criminal charges when care that is legal in New Mexico has been banned in the home state of the person travelling for it. That protection is directly relevant to a visitor arriving from a state with a care ban, and it applies alongside, not instead of, the federal document and entry rules.
tangentialFactors:
The contrast tier of the same July 2026 assessment shows how far apart the state-level positions are. States carrying the worst-ranked laws impose up to five-year prison terms, as in Idaho, or maintain an arrest policy for gender-identity bathroom use, as in Florida. A visitor crossing state lines therefore changes legal exposure within a single country, and the assessment dated 13 July 2026 records that Idaho is the latest state flagged do-not-travel for trans people, bringing the total to four states so designated, with the 2026 legislative season continuing to degrade trans rights alongside the federal measures driving nationwide trends.

Shield-law coverage is uneven nationally. Sixteen states and the District of Columbia, representing 38% of the trans population aged 13 and over, hold healthcare shields, while thirty-two states and five territories, representing 56%, hold none; youth-care bans are tracked on the same map and some have been permanently blocked. New Mexico's shield therefore sits inside a minority pattern rather than a national default, and the Movement Advancement Project's identity-document map sets out state by state which jurisdictions permit gender-marker changes on licences and birth certificates and under what conditions.
localsOnly:
Residents of New Mexico are covered by the state's shield or refuge law, which shields both patients and providers from civil or criminal charges for care legal in the state, and by the protective-tier standing the state holds in the July 2026 national legal-risk ranking. The rubric behind that ranking weighs youth-care bans, bathroom bans, birth-certificate and driver-licence restrictions and the removal of legal recognition, categories in which New Mexico is recorded on the protective side rather than the restrictive side.

State residents remain subject to the federal document regime in practice: passports and other federal identity documents reflect sex assigned at birth under Executive Order 14168, and name or gender changes interact with federal records in ways Lambda Legal's guidance addresses. The Movement Advancement Project's identity-document map is the reference for which gender-marker changes New Mexico permits on licences and birth certificates and under what conditions.
outOfScopeNotes:
The sources in this inventory do not state New Mexico's specific rules on gender markers on state driver's licences or birth certificates, its facility or bathroom rules in schools and public buildings, its hate-crime provisions, or any enforcement record of those rules. Those points are unresolved here rather than absent, and the Movement Advancement Project's identity-document map is the indicated place to verify the document position.

The July 2026 tier placement is a rubric-based ranking over tracked bills, not a citation of particular New Mexico statutes; the specific enactments behind the 'Most Protective' designation are not named in the source. The shield-law entry carries a data date of 27 September 2026 and is described on the map as a shield law or 2023 executive order, a distinction the source does not resolve. Whether the shield's protection extends to a visitor rather than a resident travelling for care is asserted as directly relevant by the source but is not tested against any New Mexico case law in this inventory.
